string.text: The seventy-four is the backbone of the line of battle: a third rate of two gun decks, heavy thirty-two-pounders below and eighteen-pounders above, with lighter guns on the quarterdeck and forecastle. She is big enough to take her place in the line against any enemy, yet handy enough to cruise far from home under a full ship rig of three masts. Her draught keeps her out of the shallows and she turns slowly, but few ships afloat can match the strength of her oak sides or the crowd of men on her decks when the enemy closes to board.

The first rate is the greatest ship of the line: three gun decks and more than a hundred guns, from thirty-two-pounders on the lower deck to twelve-pounders on the quarterdeck. She is the flagship of a fleet, built for the line of battle and for an admiral's flag, and her broadside can shatter any ship that lies alongside her. She is slow and costly, her draught keeps her out of the shallows and she needs a dockyard's care, but no enemy afloat can match her weight of metal, the thickness of her oak or the crowd of men on her decks.

The sixth rate is the smallest ship a post captain commands: a frigate-built ship of twenty-four guns, with twelve-pounders on her single gun deck and six-pounders on the quarterdeck. She has no place in the line of battle. She is the eyes of the fleet and the scourge of trade: under a full ship rig of three masts she is fast and handy, and she scouts, carries dispatches, guards convoys and hunts privateers. Her draught keeps her out of the shallows and a ship of the line can sink her in a few broadsides, but few ships that can catch her can fight her, and few that can fight her can catch her.

The great galleon is the warship of an older age, built to carry an admiral's flag and a king's treasure: a towering ship with three tiers of gun ports and seventy-four guns, twenty-four-pounders in her middle tier, twelve-pounders on her upper deck and lighter pieces in her castles. She sets a spritsail and a sprit topsail under her bowsprit and a lateen on her mizzen, and her lofty forecastle and great carved stern make her a fortress when the enemy closes to board. Beside the newer ships of the line she is slow and leewardly, and her draught keeps her out of the shallows, but she is stout, roomy and crowded with men, and few ships afloat can match her for majesty.

A fast Mediterranean warship with three lateen-rigged masts and long sweeps for calm weather. Lightly built and quick, xebecs serve Spanish coast guards and Barbary corsairs alike: they run down merchantmen, chase off smugglers and slip away from heavier ships of the line.
